title: Feeding Your Enterprise Data to a Shared LLM is a Strategic Mistake
text: Medium Feeding Your Enterprise Data to a Shared LLM is a Strategic Mistake | by Mithil Srivastav | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Mithil Srivastav The Product Guy… Product Management Product Strategy Software Engineering Product Development LLM Feeding Your Enterprise Data to a Shared LLM is a Strategic Mistake Mithil Srivastav 4 min read · 6 hours ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size A few weeks back, Chamath Palihapitiya said something most CIOs weren’t ready to hear: you can’t rent intelligence from the same place that rents it to your competitor. At first glance, that sounds like a soundbite. Of course you shouldn’t hand your crown jewels to a vendor who’s selling the same box to the company across the street. But sit with it for a moment — because that line quietly exposes the biggest blind spot in enterprise AI adoption today. Every prompt you send to a shared LLM is a small, invisible transfer of context. Your roadmap. Your pricing logic. Your customer complaints. Your unreleased code. So the real question isn’t “which model should we use?” It’s: who else is this model learning from, and who else is it serving? Renting Intelligence is Not the Same as Owning It For the last two years, enterprises have treated LLM access like they treated cloud compute — pick a vendor, plug in an API key, move fast. That worked for compute because compute is fungible. Intelligence isn’t. When you rent a model, you’re not just buying inference. You’re feeding a system that your competitor can access on the exact same terms. Chamath’s framing is blunt but correct: you cannot build a durable edge on infrastructure your rival is renting too. Owning the model — or at minimum, self-hosting it — isn’t paranoia. It’s the same instinct that made companies build their own data warehouses instead of emailing spreadsheets to a shared vendor. The Value is Moving From Models to Control Planes Here’s the uncomfortable part for the “just use GPT/Claude/Gemini” crowd: foundational models are commoditizing fast. Costs are falling. Capabilities are converging. Which means the real value isn’t sitting inside the model anymore. It’s sitting in the layer that sits between your data and the model — the harness, the router, the control plane that decides what gets sent, to whom, and what comes back. This is where enterprises should be investing: A routing layer that can swap models without leaking context Guardrails that scrub sensitive data before it ever leaves your perimeter An audit trail of every prompt and response, owned by you, not the vendor The ability to self-host open-weight models for anything sensitive If your AI strategy today is a single vendor API key with no control plane in between, you don’t have an AI strategy. You have a dependency. Bottoms-Up SaaS Adoption is Dying, and AI is the Reason Bottoms-up adoption worked when the risk was “someone expensed a $12 tool.” It doesn’t work when the risk is “someone pasted the Q3 forecast into a chatbot with no data retention policy.” The tools that survive procurement from here on will be the ones that can prove: Data never leaves the enterprise boundary No fine-tuning happens on your inputs Self-hosted or VPC-isolated deployment is available Full control over model swaps and version pinning Unvetted, consumer-grade AI tools sneaking in through individual logins won’t just get flagged. They’ll get blocked outright. Zoom out further and the same logic scales up to governments. At forums like the World Government Summit, the conversation has shifted from “how do we adopt AI” to “how do we make sure we still own our own productivity.” A nation that routes its entire economic and administrative workload through a foreign or monopolistic model provider isn’t just outsourcing a tool. It’s outsourcing a slice of its GDP and its decision-making capacity. This isn’t evolution. It’s a reckoning. Just like enterprises are realizing their data is their moat, nations are realizing their compute and model stack is their sovereignty. Self-Hosting Isn’t a Downgrade. It’s the Point. There’s a lingering myth that self-hosted models mean settling for less. Worse quality, more maintenance, slower iteration. That math is flipping. Open-weight models are closing the gap with proprietary ones every quarter. And what you lose in bleeding-edge benchmark scores, you gain back in something that doesn’t show up on a leaderboard: nobody else gets to see your data. The real trade-off was never “good model vs. bad model.” It was always “shared intelligence vs. owned intelligence.” Final Thought The next generation of enterprise AI winners won’t be the ones who adopted the flashiest model first. They’ll be the ones who asked, early: does this data leave our walls, and if it does, who else gets to learn from it? If the answer is “we don’t know” — you’re not doing AI strategy. You’re doing AI exposure.
